beats.text: Every campaign ships the same ad in a dozen shapes and languages, and designers rebuild each one by hand.
Open Apprentice learns the change from one example, asks when it is unsure, and proves every result. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron on Nebius Token Factory.

I show it once: this wide headphone banner becomes a vertical story card. The logo, product, headline, price, button and legal line all move, resize and restyle. It learns the rule by each layer's role, not by pixel positions.

On a new banner it applies the rule in a real graphics engine, Konva. An independent verifier checks the exact copy, image proportions, safe areas, minimum sizes, and whether the text fits, measured from the font itself.

Now a German banner. The headline is too long for the card. A blind tool would squeeze it, or let it overflow. Instead it stops and shows me both real options, already rendered: shrink the product image, or split the story across two cards.
I pick split. That answer is saved as a versioned preference for German, so the next long German banner is split without asking, and I can roll it back.

Real banners often arrive without labels. Nemotron, live on Nebius, looks at the layers with their names hidden, and proposes which is the headline, the price, the logo. A checker rejects impossible answers, and I confirm before anything runs.
And the same learned rule runs unchanged in a second engine, Fabric, through the same sandboxed procedure.
The same show, ask and check loop also tidies diagrams: one example, a hundred draw dot io files, every edit re-measured before it is saved.

On a sealed set of new banners in four new languages, written by a separate AI agent, every result passed, on both engines. On harder unlabeled banners, Nemotron's role proposals were right seventeen times in twenty-four; a simple size rule, seven. Nemotron proposes, checks decide, and you confirm. Open Apprentice.
